text.p: Commerzbank AG on Thursday reported a bigger-than-expected 23.2 percent rise in operating profit and tried to quash talk that the bank faces takeover or merger, saying its earnings showed it could stay independent.

Operating profit after risk provisions rose to 1.63 billion marks ($890 million) from 1.32 billion, beating analysts' forecasts which had averaged 1.44 billion marks. The bank also reaffirmed it may raise its dividend this year for the first time since 1994.
Pre-tax profit rose 24.7 percent to 1.65 billion marks from 1.32 billion.
The earnings had little impact on Commerzbank's share price, which was up 0.10 marks at 64.70 marks in early electronic dealings.
The shares have risen more than 20 percent since Friday amid speculation a Bavarian bank mega-merger announced on Monday will force it to find an ally, either at home or abroad.
Analysts say the bank is too large to be a niche player and too small to achieve the economies of scale required in an increasingly competitive sector heading for consolidation.

Commerzbank, Germany's Number Three, will be relegated to Number Four after the fusion of Bayerische Vereinsbank AG with Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG which will create the country's second largest bank.
But Commerzbank, which has been subject to recurring speculation over the past year that it may be bought by a large foreign player, again insisted it could remain independent.

"In view of the earnings performance reflected in these figures, chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen is convinced that Commerzbank can continue on its successful course and shape its future all by itself," the bank said in a statement.

It added: "There will be scope for raising the 1997 dividend while making a substantial allocation from earnings to Commerzbank's equity capital and reserves, provided that business performance remains good."
The bank paid out an unchanged dividend of 1.35 marks per share for 1996 despite a strong rise in operating profit.

Group risk provisions for loan losses rose 8.3 percent to 650 million marks from 600 million, as predicted by analysts who said provisions were likely to rise from the relatively low level a year earlier.
Commerzbank increased its risk provisions sharply in the second half of 1996.

Net interest income grew 16.5 percent to 3.34 billion marks while net commission income was up 25.5 percent at 1.45 billion, reflecting what the bank called dynamic lending and securities business in the first six months.

Net income from financial transactions fell 62 percent to 136 million marks but Commerzbank noted that earnings achieved overall in own-account securities business do not emerge clearly under German accounting methods.

If calculated under International Accounting Standards (IAS), an accounting method adopted by Deutsche Bank AG, Commerzbank's own-account trading result would have been 534 million marks in the first six months, up from 497 million.
The difference is explained by the inclusion under IAS of hidden reserves built up in proprietary trading and the inclusion of interest income related to such deals, Commerzbank said.
The balance sheet total expanded strongly by 14.5 percent to 512.9 billion marks. Lending grew 8.8 percent to 336.6 billion marks. ($ = 1.824 German Marks)
